scenes.tts: Nissl and Golgi stains show cell bodies or whole cell shapes. They do not say which protein a cell contains. Immunostaining uses an antibody against one chosen protein, so it reports molecular identity. It answers three questions. In which cells is this protein? In which part of the cell? And does it overlap with another protein?
scenes.visual: Cells shown by shape only, each marked with a question mark; an antibody lights the cells that hold the protein; three question chips appear.
scenes.narration: Nissl and Golgi stains show cell bodies or whole cell shapes. They do not say which protein a cell contains. And does it overlap with another protein?

scenes.tts: First, fix the tissue. Formaldehyde reacts with amine groups, then forms methylene bridges between neighboring groups. That locks proteins in place. Then cut the tissue into sections. Open the membranes with a detergent, so antibodies can reach inside. Then block unwanted sticking, using a protein such as B S A and normal serum.

scenes.visual: A tissue block is fixed (proteins locked by bridges in a close-up), sliced onto a slide, permeabilised so antibodies enter a cell, and blocked so sticky sites are covered.

scenes.tts: Now apply the primary antibody. It binds its epitope through the variable end. Next comes a labeled secondary antibody. It binds the constant end of the primary. A rabbit primary is found by an anti-rabbit secondary. The label is a fluorophore, or an enzyme such as horseradish peroxidase. The enzyme makes a colored product at the site. That gives a permanent preparation, seen in an ordinary microscope.
scenes.visual: Primary antibody binds target pegs by its variable end; a labeled secondary binds its constant end; the label glows (fluorophore) or an enzyme makes a colored product.

scenes.tts: Image a fluorescent slide with a fluorescence microscope. Or use a confocal, where a pinhole rejects out-of-focus light and gives optical sections that can be stacked. Use several antibodies in different colors in one section, and you see which markers coincide in one cell.
scenes.visual: Stained section imaged: an idealised image map; a pinhole blocks out-of-focus rays and sections stack; two colors in one image show one cell with both.
scenes.narration: Image a fluorescent slide with a fluorescence microscope. Or use a confocal, where a pinhole rejects out-of-focus light and gives optical sections that can be stacked. Use several antibodies in different colors in one section, and you see which markers coincide in one cell.

scenes.tts: Read the image as a map of where the protein sits. Signal in the nucleus fits a transcription factor, such as Fos. A crescent on the membrane, or signal on a lysosome surface, answers a different question. Counting stained nuclei needs a threshold and matched settings. Saturated pixels no longer report how much label is present. Where two colors overlap, the proteins lie close together. That is proximity, not interaction.
scenes.visual: Three idealised cells (nuclear, membrane crescent, lysosome surface); a saturation curve; two overlapping colors labeled proximity not interaction.

scenes.tts: Bright signal means antibody is bound, not necessarily that the protein is there. So run controls on matched tissue. Omit the primary antibody, and any signal is background, such as nonspecific binding of the secondary. Best of all, stain tissue from a knockout, processed the same way. The signal should vanish. Peptide competition, where you block the antibody with its target peptide, has limits, so use it with other controls.
scenes.visual: Stained section; then a no-primary section and a knockout section side by side; peptide competition shown with its limit.

scenes.tts: In the early 1940s, Coons's team joined antibody to a fluorescent group, so the antigen-antibody complex could be seen under ultraviolet light. In 1988, Sagar, Sharp and Curran stimulated rat cortex. Three hours later, nuclear Fos staining appeared in thalamus, pontine nuclei, globus pallidus and cerebellum. That made Fos staining a cellular map of activated pathways.
scenes.visual: Left: antigen hidden in a section, then glowing under UV with a fluorescent antibody. Right: stimulated cortex, then four regions lit with nuclear Fos at three hours.

scenes.tts: In 1994, Rhyu, Jan and Jan stained dividing Drosophila sensory organ precursor cells. The protein Numb lay on one half and passed to one daughter cell. In 2010, Sancak and colleagues showed that amino acids move m TOR C 1 to lysosomal membranes, where the Rag proteins reside. Labeling m TOR and a lysosomal protein in fixed cells showed it. A stain shows where antibody bound. Judge it against controls.
